chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said:

Al-Hakm ibn Utayba and Salama ibn Kuhayl came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and asked him about a single witness and an oath. He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) ruled by it, and Ali (peace be upon him) ruled by it in your presence in Kufa. They both said: This is contrary to the Quran! He said: And where did you find it to be contrary to the Quran? They both said: God, Blessed and Exalted, says: 'And call to witness two men of justice from among you'. So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to both of them: Does His saying 'and call to witness two men of justice from among you' mean that you should not accept the testimony of one and an oath?

Then he said: Ali (peace be upon him) was seated in the Mosque of Kufa, when Abdullah ibn Qufl al-Tamimi passed by him carrying the shield of Talha. So Ali (peace be upon him) said: This is the shield of Talha — it was taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra. So Abdullah ibn Qufl said to him: Appoint between me and you your judge, the one whom you have approved for the Muslims. So he appointed Shurayh between himself and him.

Ali (peace be upon him) said: This is the shield of Talha — it was taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra. Shurayh said to him: Bring proof for what you are saying. So he brought al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who testified that it was the shield of Talha taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra. Shurayh said: This is one witness, and I will not judge based on the testimony of one witness until there is another with him. Then he called Qanbar, who testified that it was the shield of Talha taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra. Shurayh said: This is a slave, and I will not judge based on the testimony of a slave.

He said: So Ali (peace be upon him) became angry and said: Take it! For this one has judged unjustly three times. He said: So Shurayh turned around and then said: I will not judge between two until you inform me from where I judged unjustly three times. So he said to him: Woe to you! — or fie upon you! — When I informed you that it was the shield of Talha taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra, and you said: Bring proof for what you are saying — while the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: Wherever stolen war-booty is found, it is retrieved without proof. So I said: A man who has not heard this hadith. So this is once.

Then I brought you al-Hasan and he testified, and you said: This is one, and I will not judge based on the testimony of one until there is another with him — while the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) had ruled based on the testimony of one and an oath. So this is twice.

Then I brought you Qanbar, who testified that it was the shield of Talha taken as stolen war-booty on the day of Basra, and you said: This is a slave, and I will not judge based on the testimony of a slave — yet what is wrong with the testimony of a slave when he is just?
Then he said: Woe to you! — or fie upon you! — The Imam of the Muslims is trusted regarding their affairs in matters greater than this.

key_terms.بَيِّنَة: Legal proof or evidence in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.شَاهِدٌ وَيَمِينٌ: A single witness combined with the claimant's oath — a jurisprudential ruling
key_terms.غُلُول: Illicit taking of war-booty before it is distributed; stolen war-booty
key_terms.مَمْلُوك: An owned slave whose legal testimony status was disputed

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on one witness and an oath in judicial proceedings according to the Imams?
ai.summary: This hadith presents Imam al-Baqir's (AS) defense of the legal ruling that one witness combined with the claimant's oath is a valid basis for judgment, a ruling established by the Prophet (SAWW) and practiced by Imam Ali (AS). The narrative unfolds through two interconnected episodes: a scholarly debate with al-Hakm ibn Utayba and Salama ibn Kuhayl about the Quranic verse on two witnesses, and a historical account of Ali's dispute over Talha's shield before the judge Shurayh, exposing three errors in Shurayh's reasoning — rejecting recovery of stolen war-booty without proof, rejecting single-witness testimony, and rejecting the testimony of a trusted slave. The hadith underscores Shia jurisprudential principles: prophetic rulings cannot be overridden by partial Quranic readings, and the Imam's word carries authority in matters of justice.
